title: Baron Wilkins as the political boss of Harlem
summary: Wooding says Baron controlled Harlem for Black people, controlled both parties, and protected Black cabarets with Leroy and Connors from licence denials.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: Right. Okay, now let's get to 1923 and were you still at Baron's?
I quit there at the beginning of 1923.

I had quit there and Old Man Baron said that I wouldn't be out for three days, I mean for two weeks before you wouldn't know who any of the boys was. And that's what happened. So, just like the old man said. Because the old man was a very brilliant man. He was a man that was -- it's worth saying a few words about him because he was a man that controlled

He would not let nobody else in, less it was for the black man, see? He had controlled the Democratic Party and the Republican Party. From the leaders of both parties, and old man, registered but never voted.

See, so -- but so, and he controlled both parties. Ferdinand Morton, I think was one, and I forget what the other fellow's name was now.
Anyhow -- and when Connie Carney's Inn opened up, it was called Shuffle Inn. Well, in order to protect another cabaret called Happy Rhone's, Old Man Baron wouldn't let him have a darned dancing license. And wouldn't let Connie Carney have the Shuffle Inn, as it was called then. Wouldn't let him have a dancing license, and he didn't, he wouldn't give -- where the Cotton Club was, later on, he wouldn't let that fellow sell liquor because Happy Rhone was colored cabaret.
He protected the places, he and Connors and Leroy, and all of them protected all the colored cabarets. Harlem was for a black man.
